  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Bus Driver
  trauma_type: Military
  pcl5: 53

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Screen Escape: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking, Avoid Religious Spaces: Places of worship or religious gatherings, Avoid Crowds: Crowded places such as shopping centres or public events
  Memory: Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
  Negative Appraisals: Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time
  Triggers: Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell, Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds, Auditory (Helicopter): Helicopter or aircraft sounds

Vignette:
Liam Sullivan was twenty-one when the convoy rolled through the valley, the dust choking the air before the first bang tore through it. He still remembers the sequence, though it does not always make sense when he tries to place it in a straight line. First, the sharp report, then the shudder of the ground, then the acrid scent of burning rubber and fuel rising through the open hatch. Overhead, the heavy thump of rotating blades had been a constant companion that day, and when they shifted course, the sound seemed to drop lower, closer. He knew what had happened to him; he knew the terror that had seized him in that metal cage. He simply could not find the words to give it to anyone else. Since he returned from service, those moments have settled into two distinct rhythms in his mind. Sometimes they arrive as fragmented pieces, disconnected shards of light and sound that do not fit together. Other times, they play over and over like a film reel, exact and unchanging, forcing him to relive the heat and the shockwave as if they are happening now. Liam had come to believe that the world was a dangerous place. He needed to be on guard all the time, his eyes tracking the horizon, his shoulders tensing when a door slammed too hard, his attention cataloguing every potential threat as it arrived. This constant vigilance existed alongside his avoidance of religious spaces, where he would step past arched doorways and stone interiors, uneasy with the echoes and the high ceilings. Crowds felt equally exposed. Shopping centres and public events pressed in on him, the density of bodies and movement making it impossible to keep his bearings. Liam began spending long hours on his phone. He lost himself in games and the endless scroll of the internet, using these stretches to avoid thinking. This screen escape sat quietly beside his other habits, a way of filling the space between threats. Now, his work as a bus driver has become a specific testing ground. His routes take him through busy corridors where the bus’s own brakes sometimes release a sharp, burnt scent that catches him off guard, sending his pulse spiking before he can steady himself. He hears construction bangs and low-flying aircraft near the depot, and each sound pulls him back to that valley. When he is on the road, he watches his mirrors, checks his blind spots, and measures his acceleration, his body still holding the memory of the shudder. At home, his apartment sits quietly, but the screen’s glow is his constant companion. He lies on his couch long after his shift, thumb scrolling, eyes fixed, until the silence finally settles. He is single, and though he has not tried to date since the service, he feels less sure that life is worth living. The future looks like a long stretch of unexplained noise and guarded moments, and he wonders how much longer he can keep holding himself tight. It was the accumulation of these days that finally brought him to a clinic last month. A particularly loud bus backfire had made him pull over and sit in the driver’s seat for twenty minutes, unable to move, while the burnt smell of the brakes lingered in the cab. He realized then that he was no longer simply surviving his route; he was bracing for an impact that would never come. He sought help not because he expected the memories to vanish, but because he needed to understand what was happening to him. He hopes to find a way to let the world back in, to stop scanning every sound and scent, and to finally explain what he has carried without words. What frightens him most is that the film reel will keep playing forever, and that he will miss the rest of his life while waiting for the next bang.
